lead: Both readings ask what a Christian owes to the state, and both answer by placing the state under God. Paul tells the Christians in Rome that every lawful authority has its place from God and serves the common good, so taxes and obedience are a matter of conscience. In Matthew, Jesus is asked a trap question about the Roman tax; he asks whose image is on the coin, and gives an answer that has guided the Church ever since: give the emperor what is his, and give God what is God’s. The coin bears Caesar’s image; the human person bears God’s.

r.h: There is no authority except from God
set: Paul wrote Romans from Corinth, probably around AD 57, to a Church he had not yet visited. Nero was emperor, in the calm early years of his reign. The Christians of Rome were a small group with no power, some of them Jews who had been expelled under Claudius and had returned (Acts 18:2). The Roman historian Tacitus reports loud complaints in the city about indirect taxes around AD 58. Paul has just told his readers not to repay evil for evil and to leave vengeance to God (12:17–21). Now he speaks of the ruler who punishes wrongdoing as God’s servant for the common good.
str: vv. 1–2: every person should be subject; all authority comes from God; to resist it is to resist God’s order.
vv. 3–4: rulers exist to restrain evil and encourage good; the authority is “God’s servant for your good”.
v. 5: obey not only from fear of punishment but for the sake of conscience.
v. 6: this is also why you pay taxes.
kw: Literally “to place oneself under”, to accept one’s place in an order. It is not blind obedience to anything a ruler commands, but respect for the order that God wills for life in society.
Paul calls the civil authority by the same word he uses for ministers of the Gospel. The ruler is a servant, not a master, and he is accountable to God for the good of the people.
The inner judgment by which a person knows right and wrong before God. Paul grounds civic duty in conscience; the same conscience can also tell a Christian when a command must be refused (Acts 5:29).
vv: Let every person be subject to the governing authorities; for there is no authority except from God
Paul does not say that every ruler is good, but that authority as such belongs to God’s plan for human life together. Rulers receive their power in trust.
for it is God’s servant for your good.
Here is the measure of all authority: the good of those it serves. An authority that works against the good of its people departs from its own purpose.
Therefore one must be subject, not only because of wrath but also because of conscience.
A Christian is an honest citizen even when no one is watching, because he obeys God.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses when it teaches that every human community needs an authority, and that authority has its source in God (CCC 1897–1899). It adds that authority is exercised legitimately only when it seeks the common good by morally lawful means; if rulers enact unjust laws, these do not bind in conscience (CCC 1903). Citizens owe rulers respect, taxes and a share in the common good (CCC 2238–2240), and they are obliged in conscience not to follow civil commands that are contrary to the moral order, for “We must obey God rather than any human authority” (CCC 2242; Acts 5:29). Paul himself, who wrote these lines, was later put to death under the same emperor, faithful to Christ to the end.

set: Jesus is in the Temple in Jerusalem during his last days before the Passion. After three parables against the leaders (21:28–22:14), they try to trap him. Two groups who were usually opposed join together: some disciples of the Pharisees, who resented Roman rule, and the Herodians, supporters of the house of Herod, who depended on Rome. The tax in question was the poll tax paid directly to Rome, a sore sign of foreign rule. If Jesus said “Pay it”, he could lose the people; if he said “Do not pay”, he could be reported to the governor as a rebel.
str: vv. 15–17: the plot and the flattering question: is it lawful to pay the tax to the emperor?
vv. 18–19: Jesus sees their malice and asks for the coin.
vv. 20–21: “Whose head is this?” “The emperor’s.” Give to the emperor and give to God.
v. 22: they are amazed and go away.
kw: From the Latin census: the tax counted per head. It had to be paid in Roman coin.

The silver denarius of Tiberius carried his portrait and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus. The word is the one used in the Greek Old Testament for man made “in the image” of God (Genesis 1:27).
Not simply “give” but “give back”, pay what is owed. The coin already belongs to Caesar; the person already belongs to God.
vv: Teacher, we know that you are sincere, and teach the way of God in accordance with truth
The flattery is meant to push him into a dangerous answer. Yet what they say is true, more true than they know.
Show me the coin used for the tax.
Jesus does not carry the coin himself; his questioners produce it, in the Temple. Their own pockets give the answer.
Give therefore to the emperor the things that are the emperor’s, and to God the things that are God’s.
The two halves are not equal. Caesar may claim coins; God claims the whole person. The state has a real place, but it is not God.
ch: The Catechism quotes this saying when it teaches the duty of citizens and its limit: when the commands of civil authority are contrary to the moral order, the citizen must refuse, for one must give to Caesar what is Caesar’s and to God what is God’s (CCC 2242). Tertullian drew out the meaning of the image: give the coin with Caesar’s image to Caesar, and give to God yourself, who bear God’s image (in substance, On Idolatry 15). The Second Vatican Council teaches that the political community and the Church are independent in their own fields, yet both serve the same human persons (Gaudium et Spes 76).

qa: Does Romans 13 mean Christians must obey any government, even a cruel one?

No. Paul describes what authority is for: to reward good and restrain evil. The Church teaches that laws contrary to the moral order do not bind in conscience, and that citizens must refuse commands that go against God’s law (CCC 1903, 2242). The apostles themselves told the council in Jerusalem, “We must obey God rather than any human authority” (Acts 5:29). Christians obey lawful authority out of conscience, and for the same reason they may not obey it in what is evil.
study: Paul calls the ruler “God’s servant for your good”. How can I pray for and support those who govern, and also help them serve the common good?
If the coin belongs to Caesar because it bears his image, what does it mean that I bear God’s image? What in my life have I not yet given back to God?
